title: Looking at Assessments Differently
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino reworks her approach to classroom assessments after a Year 10 student's comment - "why do teachers always say I did well? When I get my test back, I've got less than 50%" - forced her to confront a mismatch between her reassurances and how students were actually experiencing test results. She reflects honestly on her own past framing of assessments, admitting to language like "how could you have gotten this question wrong when I have explained it so many times" that she now recognizes as feeding student anxiety rather than motivating effort. Revisiting the familiar observation that students perform better on second mock exams than first, she reframes it: rather than crediting a post-shock work-ethic improvement, she attributes at least part of the gain to students having simply rehearsed the process of sitting a mock exam once already, making the second attempt more executable regardless of content mastery. Her redesigned approach treats assessment preparation as three distinct trainable skills threaded throughout a topic rather than crammed at the end - ongoing revision technique modelled through tools like labelled mini-whiteboard diagrams, practice interpreting exam-style questions under teacher guidance, and separately, practice performing under timed, silent conditions - with the explicit message to students that the score matters less than how they engage with the process of answering.
points: Castelino traces her shift in thinking about assessments to a single student's comment - "why do teachers always say I did well? When I get my test back, I've got less than 50%" - which exposed a gap between her intended encouragement and how it actually landed.

She reinterprets the well-known second-mock-exams-go-better pattern not as students simply trying harder after a wake-up call, but as a rehearsal effect: having practised the process of sitting a mock once makes the second attempt genuinely easier to execute.
Castelino is unusually candid about her own contribution to student anxiety, quoting her past phrasing as an example of language she now recognizes as harmful.

Her redesigned approach treats assessments as three separable skills to build across a topic - revision technique, exam-question interpretation, and timed/silent performance conditions - rather than a single end-of-topic test of content knowledge.
quotes: One of my students was really worried- they struggle to remember facts despite really trying in lessons and doing their homework each week. They get quite anxious about assessments.
why do teachers always say I did well? When I get my test back, I’ve got less than 50%

I used to think this was mostly because the first round of Mocks would surprise students as to how much effort is required in order to do well and they start building in better habits and revising more. But recently, I have started to see that one of the reasons for the increase in performance is the fact they have practised the process of completing a Mock exam once

This negative mindset was influencing my students. I would say things like ‘this assessment is very important because I can see if you’ve been revising at home’ or ‘how could you have gotten this question wrong when I have explained it so many times!?
Sometimes, a student who has slowly built up good study habits with much struggle may revert to older, ineffective habits when anxious about being judged by a grade or outcome.

I talk about revision throughout the topic so it isn’t something we simply do at the end of a topic to prepare for an assessment. I model self-study techniques such as writing and drawing labelled diagrams from memory on mini-whiteboards.
The score is not as important as the performance in answering questions.
